title: The Gayatri at dawn
hookLine: Rama woken for the dawn prayer; sandhya
carry: sandhya: the gayatri, kept at dawn

lines: A MAN IN THE RIVER, FACING EAST.
cards: Before dawn, on the steps down to the river at Varanasi, a man stands waist-deep in the water, facing east.

He cups water in his hands, and as the first edge of the sun comes up, he lifts it and says a few lines under his breath. Far away in New Jersey, a boy with a new thread across his chest sets an alarm for the same hour.
Same words, far older than either of them: the Gayatri. You learned on day three what it asks for. Today, why it's kept at dawn.

teach.b: The Ramayana has a quiet moment that shows it. The sage Vishvamitra, the seer tradition credits with the Gayatri, has taken two boys from the palace, Rama and his brother Lakshmana. They sleep on a riverbank.
Before sunrise the old sage bends over them and wakes them, in a verse that still opens the morning song at many temples: Rama, Kausalya's blessed son, the eastern sandhya, the dawn, is coming.
Get up; the day's rites to the gods are waiting.
And the princes rise, bathe in the river, offer water, and do their japa. Many teachers say what they chanted was the Gayatri. Here's the teaching.
Sandhya: the junction, where night meets day, and the name of the dawn prayer itself.

Traditionally the Gayatri is given to a child at the upanayana, the sacred thread ceremony, and from then on it's kept at the junctions of the day: facing the rising sun, offering water from cupped hands, asking the sun's light to wake the mind.
Traditions differ on who chants it. Many keep it for those who have received the thread; many modern teachers and movements open it to everyone.
Both views are held by devout Hindus; its meaning in English belongs to anyone. Now notice Rama. In the tradition he's God born human, and still his teacher wakes him in the dark to pray.
The Gayatri isn't saved for a crisis. It's kept like a promise, at the same hour, before anything else gets the mind.

teach.h: SANDHYA: THE GAYATRI, KEPT AT DAWN.
teach.b: Sandhya: the Gayatri, kept at dawn.

how: Many Hindus chant the Gayatri at dawn and dusk as part of sandhya worship, often facing the sun and offering water; traditionally it is taught at the upanayana (sacred thread) ceremony, while many modern teachers and movements share it with all.

o: the goddess of rivers, honored at Varanasi at dawn
a Rig Veda verse asking the sun to light up the mind
a morning hymn asking the sun for a good harvest

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: the junction where night meets day
the sage who woke Rama at dawn
the sun that stirs things awake

s: as a prince, Rama was excused from the dawn prayers
his teacher woke him before sunrise, and he bathed, offered water and did his japa.
the Gayatri is traditionally given at the sacred thread ceremony
and from then on it's kept at the junctions of the day, dawn first.
all Hindus agree anyone may chant it
many keep it for those who received the thread; others open it to everyone. both views are held by devout Hindus.

games.q: your cousin just had his thread ceremony. it's 6 a.m., he's exhausted, and he asks if the Gayatri can wait till after school. what does the tradition say?
o: any time of day is the same.
it's kept at the junction, as the sun comes up.
games.why: sandhya means the junction, where night meets day. even Rama's teacher woke him in the dark for it.

practice: Sit facing a window if you can, or picture the sun just coming up. If your tradition welcomes you to chant it, say the last line softly, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat; if not, hold its meaning in English: light, illuminate the mind.
Say it once, then hold it the way you'd hold your face toward the morning sun, and say it again when your attention drifts.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri. A verse to the sun who stirs everything awake, kept at the junctions of the day, asking it to light up our minds.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the verse's meter, and of the Goddess the verse became.

carryVoice: Carry this: sandhya, the Gayatri, kept at dawn. Even Rama got up in the dark for it. That's day one hundred eight.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 3.62.10 (the Gayatri mantra; the vyahritis bhur bhuvah svah said before it)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (sarga 23 in common editions): Vishvamitra wakes Rama at dawn, 'kausalya supraja rama'; the princes bathe and do their japa
